Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-memory See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Background and motivation With #33244 and #63547, we now have the new `NativeMemory` type exposing lowlevel building blocks to perform common operations on memory. The APIs in this type are thing wrappers over the relative C API, and they all accept raw pointers and `nuint` length as parameters. They're effectively the "correct" (or, "easy", "preferred", "modern", whatever) way to interact with raw memory going forward, especially for people trying to migrate code from C/C++. They also remove ambiguity when having to do an operation that has otherwise multiple ways to be expressed in C#, such as clearing memory. Do I use `new Span(...).Clear()`? Do I use `Unsafe.InitBlock`? If I want to copy memory, do I use `new Span(...).CopyTo`? Do I use `Buffer.MemoryCopy`? Do I use `Unsafe.CopyBlock`? Going forward instead, it's quite easy: if you have a raw pointer, then `NativeMemory` is the way to go. Easy, no confusion, and consistent behavior for all APIs. This proposal is about adding the "missing" APIs to `NativeMemory` to complete the set. These are: - `memset` - `memcopy` - `memmove` - `memcmp` cc. @tannergooding ### API Proposal ```csharp namespace System.Runtime.InteropServices; public static class NativeMemory { public static void SetMemory(void* ptr, byte value, nuint byteCount); public static int CompareMemory(void* ptr1, void* ptr2, nuint byteCount); public static void CopyMemory(void* destination, void* source, nuint byteCount); public static void MoveMemory(void* destination, void* source, nuint byteCount); } ``` Exact names are up to discussion I assume, I used the .NET convention here but we might also want to eg. use `Memset` instead of `SetMemory`, and `Memcmp` instead of `CompareMemory`, etc. I guess there's arguments for both, so leaving this to FXDC. ### API Usage Same use case scenario as where the relative C APIs would normally be used. ### Alternative Designs Keep using different APIs scattered all over the place, with inconsistent behavior, and not all accepting `nuint` lengths. ### Risks None, really.
Author: Sergio0694
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-System.Memory`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -
I'd propose dropping _memcpy_ and exposing only _memmove_, but otherwise LGTM. We can expose _memcpy_ in the future if there's a real hardcore scenario for it.

Can't all these be done using existing APIs on `Span<T>`?

> Can't all these be done using existing APIs on `Span<T>`?

Not if you have a byteCount > int.MaxValue.

> Can't all these be done using existing APIs on `Span<T>`?

@AaronRobinsonMSFT Kind of, but it's a bit weird without true nint support on `Span<T>`. The caller would have to create helpers to call the existing `Span<T>` methods in a loop.

Also how would you do `memcmp` and `memcpy` with `Span<T>`?
AFAIK `Span<T>.CopyTo` is equivalent to `memmove` (as it has extra logic to handle overlaps).
As for `memcmp`, wouldn't you need some additional logic to find the first not equal `byte` and then compare it? 🤔
I guess there's also the argument of having a single, consistent "goto" set of APIs for memory manipulation.
Tanner also mentioned one of the points was also to offer thing wrappers of the underlying APIs, and to help people porting code.

Right. One benefit is that we can contract these APIs to just be calls to the CRT.

This simplifies a lot of things including when/where to call it and covers the scenario where we already have and use such APIs internally for some of the Span<T> or other variants.

Calling into the CRT yourself is complex and potentially error prone, particularly when needing to consider various library names/versions, where APIs are split, etc.

You then have `Span<T>` for managed or small unmanaged and `NativeMemory` for large unmanaged.

> Not if you have a byteCount > int.MaxValue.
> @AaronRobinsonMSFT Kind of, but it's a bit weird without true nint support on Span<T>.

Then it would appear if we add `nint` support, these methods could be done using the `Span<T>` methods. Which seems like what we want users to reach for, right?

> You then have Span<T> for managed or small unmanaged and NativeMemory for large unmanaged.

This argument doesn't sit well with me. Adding `nint` support to `Span<T>` does sound like it would enable the "just use Span<T>" statement to hold. Is there a reason this wasn't done?

> Is there a reason this wasn't done?

Its a very large breaking change because every `for (int i = 0; i < span.Length; i++)` loop is now potentially broken.

We might be able to mitigate that by having `Span<T>.Length` and `Span<T>.NativeLength` where the former basically does `return checked((int)NativeLength)` and the majority of spans continue working, but it still leaves the "hole" where you don't know whether or not a given method supports large spans or not.

Likewise, `Span<T>` while good for managed isn't nearly as efficient or as optimized as the underlying CRT functions, particularly for large data.

We could certainly update them to correctly use non-temporal loads/stores and vectorized comparisons everywhere but that's quite a lot of work and there has been pushback in the past on if the long term maintenance for that is worthwhile over just having users defer to native for the "edge cases"

> Span<T> while good for managed isn't nearly as efficient or as optimized as the underlying CRT functions, particularly for large data.

`Span<T>` [delegates to the CRT for large buffers](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/search?q=MemmoveNativeThreshold) for these functions as appropriate, for the reasons you have mentioned. We handle the smaller buffers in managed code to avoid the transition cost for them. I expect we would use the exact same implementation for these APIs (ie these APIs would be one-liner wrappers of the existing worker methods used for Span.

> SetMemory

This should be called `FillMemory` for consistency with similar existing APIs.

> I'd propose dropping memcpy

+1. The undefined behavior of `memcpy` for overlapping buffers is a common source of breaks when upgrading C/C++ compilers or porting to new platforms. We do not need this breaking change farm in .NET.

I would call the API `CopyMemory` for consistency with similar existing APIs.

> CompareMemory

This is the least useful API from this set. We may want to omit it from this batch too. There are other similar APIs in terms of usefulness (e.g. `memchr`). Unclear how we are going to decide which ones to include once we get to these less frequently used ones.

> "This should be called FillMemory for consistency with similar existing APIs."

Just to clarify, didn't we want the APIs in `NativeMemory` to have names matching the underlying C APIs as much as possible? As in, that was my understanding given that eg. the one to clear is also called `ZeroMemory` and not `ClearMemory` 🤔

Same goes for `CopyMemory` to wrap `memmove` too I guess.

> As in, that was my understanding given that eg. the one to clear is also called ZeroMemory and not ClearMemory

The matching C++ API is caller `memset`. I see no similarity between `ZeroMemory` and `memset`. (There is Windows-specific `ZeroMemory` macro in Windows SDK that is `#define`d to memset. Windows SDK names are not necessarily the best prior art for .NET naming.)

Good point though. We may want to rename `ZeroMemory` to `ClearMemory` for consistency.

> Same goes for CopyMemory to wrap memmove too I guess.

All `Copy*` APIs for copying memory in .NET (Array.Copy, Span,Copy, Buffer.MemoryCopy, ...) handle overlapping buffers. I do not see a good reason for this one to be an outlier.

@Sergio0694 This seems fine for .NET 7 if we can get the proposal updated with the feedback above and shepherded through API review. I've marked this as Future but can switch it back if someone other than the Interop team is planning on moving it forward.

Sweet, sounds good to me! I guess we just need @tannergooding to get back and share his thoughts on the new comments in here, then I can update the proposal and we can go to API review this week. I'd also be happy to help with the implementation in case other folks are too slammed (eg. I know Tanner has quite his hands full with all the generic math stuff lately 😄).

The proposed changes make sense to me for API review.

I do think there is benefit to more closely matching the existing native names, but not enough that its worth pushing on.

> given we also already have Alloc, Realloc etc. instead of something more .NET-like, such as Allocate or whatever

These names match the existing .NET APIs on interop related types: `Marshal.AllocCoTaskMem`, `Marshal.ReallocCoTaskMem`, `GCHandle.Alloc`, ... .

> That said I guess the current API set is already a bit of a mashup given that eg. we also repeat "Memory" only in some cases.

Yes, the `Memory` is repeated for the `ZeroMemory`. We should have spent more a bit more time on this name - to avoid the redundant `Memory` and to make the name consistent with similar APIs on other types.

My suggestion would be: `NativeMemory.Copy`, `NativeMemory.Clear`, `NativeMemory.Fill`

- .NET convention is to have source first on `Copy` methods
- Fill arguments are wrong (copy&paste)

> .NET convention is to have source first on Copy methods

We have a range of this. For example `Unsafe.Copy/CopyBlock` does `destination` first since that's what IL uses.

I'd personally lean towards matching native here given its under `NativeMemory` and do `destination` first. We're in an unfortunate situation where some group of people will get this wrong likely no matter what we do.

Just noticed that modern C++ has destination last in `std::copy`: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/copy

> where some group of people will get this wrong likely no matter what we do.

Yep. I think that argues for maximizing consistency within .NET and ignoring what's done elsewhere.

> We're in an unfortunate situation where some group of people will get this wrong likely no matter what we do.

Yup. I would propose that our internal usage of this and any documentation uses named parameters. Get people - including our own devs - in the habit of doing this. Make it second nature and minimize the chance of errors.
I have updated the API proposal and marked this as blocking so that we get a chance to reconsider the `ZeroMemory` name before it ships.
@jkotas , could you please assign this task to me? I'm already working on it in #72960

@teo-tsirpanis , thanks! Can I ask about some guidance from your side about implementation? I'm a bit stuck on `Fill` implementation. I see that appropriate PAL method is for Unix-like OS only: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Unix/System.Native/Interop.MemSet.cs

However, I don't see any reason why not to reuse it on other operating systems because `memset` is a part of standard C library: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/native/libs/System.Native/pal_memory.c. Moreover, the necessary function is already exported for all OSes: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/native/libs/System.Native/entrypoints.c

So from my point of view, the change is trivial: just move `Interop.MemSet.cs` to appropriate location available to all platforms. In the same time, AOT has a separate import of the function: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/coreclr/nativeaot/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Runtime/RuntimeImports.cs

What is the best way to access `memset` function?

You need to write one implementation for Windows and one for Unix, just like what we already do for the allocation APIs in `NativeMemory.Windows.cs` and `NativeMemory.Unix.cs`. On Windows we reference the standard C library through the [`Interop.Ucrtbase`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/tree/main/src/libraries/Common/src/Interop/Windows/Ucrtbase) class.
For `Fill`, you should call `SpanHelpers.Fill<byte>`. I doubt that any CRT memset implementation would be able to beat it.

@jkotas , @danmoseley , FYI, I didn't find any usage of `SystemNative_MemSet` across the code base. The import declared incorrectly and source generator cannot generate the code for it. Moreover, it is not a part of compilation item in `System.Private.CoreLib.Shared.projitems`. Probably, it can be removed in future (and from PAL C code as well).

> `SystemNative_MemSet` 

Could you please delete it as part of your PR?
@jkotas , sure, no problem.

> I doubt that any CRT memset implementation would be able to beat it.

@jkotas, I'd actually expect for larger buffers that the `CRT` implementation may report measurably better still.

Most of the CRT implementations take into account alignment, non-temporal loads/stores, and can use `rep stos` where it's faster.

However, given that being in a P/Invoke or having data pinned for that long can have negative impact on the GC and that the transition cost/call overhead is high for small data, I expect we want to have some of it handled in managed at least.

---------------------------

The Win x64 implementations which are source available (but not OSS licensed) are here: `C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\VC\Tools\MSVC\14.32.31326\crt\src\x64`. The cutoffs it uses are:
* Less than 16-bytes - use GPR
* 16-32 bytes use 1-2 128-bit SIMD stores, possibly overlapping
* 33-8k bytes use 256-bit or 128-bit SIMD stores
* 8k-256k use `rep stos` if available, else 256-bit or 128-bit SIMD stores
* Greater than 256k use `non-temporal`

Given we have `Vector128.StoreUnsafe` and `Vector128.StoreAlignedNonTemporal` as a general xplat APIs, we could (maybe for .NET 8) have a single implementation that nicely supports x64 and Arm64 without needing to make it overly advanced. We likewise could add minimal handling in the JIT to ensure that small copies/fills (at least <= 32 bytes) are directly inlined. Optimizing x64 and Arm64 to use the respective `rep stos`/`cpymx` instructions where supported (avoiding the calls entirely and deferring to the optimized CPU impls).

Yeah, the current impl is probably leaving some perf of the ground for very large sizes. 

> cpymx

I can't wait for this to become mainstream hw feature.
@jkotas , what is the strategy for the current implementation? We can continue to use `SpanHelpers` or add optimizations for small sizes + fallback to CRT functions instead.

Use SpanHelpers. 

The potential future optimizations should be done in SpanHelpers so that all callers of SpanHelpers benefit.

review_comments: I'd like to see some values that aren't related to powers of 2.

what is expected behavior for overlaps? it is unclear to me from the discussion in the issue, but it seemed that it was undesirable that it be undefined or crash, in which case we should have tests presumably.
According to discussion, `Copy` follows behavior of `memove` native implementation. It supports memory overlapping.
